findings.summary: RAW_TEXT_OIDS only covers scalar DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ; array and range date/time types still get parsed into JS `Date` and remain timezone-shifted
findings.evidence: `RAW_TEXT_OIDS = new Set([DATE, TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMPTZ])` and `datasourceTypeParser` falls through to the default parser for every other OID. pg-types registers parsers for the array OIDs 1182 (date[]), 1115 (timestamp[]), 1185 (timestamptz[]) and for range types (3908 tsrange, 3910 tstzrange, 3912 daterange) that build JS `Date` objects for each element via the same local-time parse the comment says is wrong. A `SELECT ARRAY['2025-06-15 14:30:00'::timestamp]` therefore still returns Dates; those are JSON-serialized (toISOString/toJSON, UTC) after having been parsed in the Node runtime's timezone, so the exact off-by-offset bug this change fixes for scalars persists for arrays/ranges — and `toCell` then JSON.stringify's them, yielding shifted ISO strings in cells. The fix is incomplete for the stated invariant "no date/time value is reinterpreted in the Node timezone".

findings.summary: Forcing `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` also changes date *input* interpretation and can silently produce wrong results for user queries written against a DMY server
findings.evidence: `await client.query(`SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'`)` is run unconditionally before the user's SELECT. DateStyle controls both output formatting (the intent here) and the ordering used when parsing ambiguous date literals. A user query containing e.g. `WHERE d = '15/06/2025'` (valid on a server configured DMY) will now either error or, for ambiguous values like `'06/07/2025'`, be interpreted as June 7 instead of July 6 — silently wrong rows returned. Only the output half is needed; the input reinterpretation is an unintended behavioral change for existing saved queries.

findings.summary: Leftover duplicate `it('queries real tables with rows')` — the old version of the test the diff intended to replace is still present
findings.evidence: The new test is added at line 114 and an identical-named older test survives at line 309, both creating/TRUNCATE-ing/DROP-ing the same `_test_products` table and asserting the same query. This looks like a bad merge: the diff added the rewritten copy without deleting the original. Both bodies run (duplicate names are legal in jest), so the suite does the same DDL twice and any future divergence between the two copies is easy to miss; the surviving copy also still asserts the pre-change shape `{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: '9.99' }`.

findings.summary: 'converts query runtime failures to bad request' no longer exercises the user-query failure path — the mock now throws on the new `SET TimeZone` statement
findings.evidence: The mock only special-cases `sql.startsWith('SET statement_timeout')` and throws for everything else. With the two new session statements added at datasource.service.ts:144-145, the rejection now happens on `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'`, i.e. before `client.query(wrappedQuery)` is ever reached. The test still passes but no longer covers the branch it names (a real query error being mapped to BadRequestException).

findings.summary: `toCell` renders Buffer/bytea values as `{"type":"Buffer","data":[...]}`, an unusable and potentially enormous cell string
findings.evidence: `if (typeof val === 'object' && val !== null) return JSON.stringify(val);` — a pg BYTEA column comes back as a Buffer (or, over HTTP, as its JSON form `{type:'Buffer',data:[…]}`), so each byte becomes 2-4 characters of cell text. The e2e test at database.e2e-spec.ts:219 enshrines exactly this output. For a non-trivial bytea column this produces multi-megabyte cell values (memory/render cost) instead of e.g. a hex string.

findings.summary: Newly exported `toCell` turns nullish input into the literal strings 'null'/'undefined'; the null guard lives only in its one internal caller
findings.evidence: `toCell` is now part of the public sheets API (exported from packages/sheets/src/index.ts:197) but has no nullish handling: `String(null)` → 'null'. The only protection is `if (val === null || val === undefined) continue;` at readonly.ts:71 inside `loadQueryResults`. Any other caller (the backend e2e test already calls it directly at database.e2e-spec.ts:175/301) will write 'null' into a cell where an empty cell is meant.

findings.summary: `types.getTypeParser` is captured detached from its module object
findings.evidence: `const getDefaultParser = types.getTypeParser as (...)` stores an unbound reference and later calls it as `getDefaultParser(oid, format)`. pg-types' current implementation does not use `this`, so this works today, but it silently breaks if the upstream implementation ever becomes method-style; `types.getTypeParser(oid, format)` at the call site would be safe unconditionally.

findings.summary: Assertions weakened by `String(...)` coercion, hiding the actual value type the parser change affects

findings.summary: `toCell` is a generic value→string serializer exported from a store module and now consumed by the backend test; layer/placement is questionable
findings.evidence: `toCell` has nothing to do with the Store interface — it is a generic unknown→string conversion. Putting it in `store/readonly.ts` and re-exporting it from the sheets public API (`packages/sheets/src/index.ts`) makes the backend e2e suite depend on the sheet engine purely for a 4-line helper. Shared conversion helpers of this kind are the sort of thing this repo puts in `@wafflebase/core` (or, within sheets, alongside `model/worksheet/format.ts` which already owns value formatting). findings.summary: Redundant handling: the pg parser override makes `toCell`'s `Date` branch dead for datasource results
findings.evidence: The service now returns DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ as raw strings, so query-result values can no longer be `Date` for those OIDs. `toCell`'s `val instanceof Date` → `toISOString()` branch therefore encodes a second, conflicting policy (UTC ISO with `T`/`Z`) for a case the backend change was introduced to eliminate. Two overlapping mechanisms for the same concern; pick one and document it.

findings.summary: Three sequential round-trips per query for session setup where one statement (or a connection `options` string) would do
findings.evidence: `await client.query(statement_timeout)` / `SET TimeZone` / `SET DateStyle` are three separate awaited round-trips on a connection that the design doc explicitly notes is created and destroyed per query ('No connection pooling', datasource.md:202). These could be a single `SET` batch or passed as libpq `options: '-c timezone=UTC ...'` on the Client config next to the other connection options, avoiding added per-query latency.

findings.summary: ~50-row hard-coded matrix of Postgres built-in OIDs is broader scope than the date/time change under review and is version-brittle
findings.evidence: The new 'check correct cell values for all pg built-in types' test asserts exact cell strings for BYTEA/CIRCLE/INTERVAL/MONEY/TSVECTOR/REGPROC/PG_LSN etc., plus expected `dataTypeID` per type, and carries a commentary block about which OIDs were removed in PG12/13. The change being made concerns DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ only; the rest pins pg-types' default parsers and locale-dependent output (e.g. MONEY `'$1,234.56'` depends on lc_monetary) into this repo's contract, which will break on unrelated pg/PostgreSQL upgrades. Consider narrowing to the types this change actually affects.

findings.summary: Datasource TLS connections disable certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), so a network attacker can MITM and capture the decrypted datasource credentials
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:202 — `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. This is the same `createClient` object literal the diff modifies (it adds `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` at line 204). Vector: a user enables `sslEnabled` believing the connection is authenticated; an attacker on the path between backend and remote Postgres (or who can poison DNS for the user-supplied `host`) presents a self-signed cert. Node accepts it, and the backend then sends `user` plus `decrypt(ds.password)` (line 201) over the attacker-terminated TLS session, handing over plaintext DB credentials and all query results. No CA/hostname option exists in the DTO (datasource.dto.ts has only `sslEnabled`), so verified TLS is unreachable for any caller.

findings.summary: SSRF: fully user-controlled `host`/`port` are dialed by the server and connection errors are reflected verbatim, allowing internal port/service probing and unix-socket access to the app's own database
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.dto.ts:17-25 validates `host` only as a 1-253 char string and `port` only as 1-65535 — no allow-list and no rejection of `localhost`, RFC1918, `169.254.169.254`, or `/var/run/postgresql` (pg treats a host starting with `/` as a unix socket path). Any authenticated workspace member POSTs `/workspaces/:id/datasources` then `/datasources/:id/test`; `testConnection` (datasource.service.ts:109-125) returns `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }` straight to the caller, so ECONNREFUSED vs. timeout vs. 'invalid response to SSL negotiation' distinguishes open/closed/non-Postgres internal ports — an internal port scanner with an error oracle. Pointing `host` at the loopback/unix socket plus trust auth or guessed creds reaches the application's own Postgres (all users/tokens). `executeQuery` (line 168) likewise reflects raw pg errors. Pre-existing, but it is the connection path this diff edits and the new e2e tests drive end to end.

findings.summary: Read-only enforcement is a SQL keyword blocklist only; the newly added session `SET` block omits `default_transaction_read_only`, so side-effecting functions inside a SELECT can still write to the connected database
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:143-145 now issues three session settings (`statement_timeout`, `TimeZone`, `DateStyle`) but not `SET default_transaction_read_only = on` / `SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, the only enforcement Postgres itself honours. Enforcement therefore rests entirely on packages/backend/src/datasource/sql-validator.ts:1-13, a substring blocklist of DML keywords. A workspace member — not necessarily the credential owner, since `/datasources/:id/query` only requires `assertMember` (datasource.controller.ts:133-145) — can submit `SELECT * FROM (SELECT my_volatile_writer()) x`, `SELECT nextval('some_seq')`, `SELECT lo_import('/etc/passwd')`, `SELECT pg_read_file(...)` or `SELECT dblink(...)`: none contain a forbidden keyword, all pass validation and are executed at line 150 inside the `SELECT * FROM (...)` wrapper, producing writes, local file reads (superuser) or outbound connections on the remote database.
searchedFor: read datasource.service.ts and datasource.controller.ts in full for other enforcement layers
glob packages/backend/src/datasource/** to enumerate the module

findings.summary: The `statement_timeout` guard may be neutralised from inside the submitted SELECT via `set_config`, enabling long-running query DoS
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:143 sets `statement_timeout` as a separate session statement, then line 150 executes the user query. The validator does not block `set_config`, so `WITH t AS (SELECT set_config('statement_timeout','0',false)) SELECT pg_sleep(600) FROM t` passes validation (starts with WITH, no forbidden keyword, single statement). If Postgres re-evaluates the GUC rather than keeping the timer armed from statement start, each request pins a backend connection and a remote session indefinitely; repeated requests exhaust connections on both sides. I could not confirm PostgreSQL's mid-statement timer behaviour from the repo, hence low confidence — but nothing in the code prevents the attempt.

findings.summary: `create` and `update` return the datasource row including the encrypted password blob, unlike `findOne`/`findAllByWorkspace` which mask it
findings.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:44-56 (`create`) and 95-98 (`update`) return the Prisma record as-is, so the AES-256-GCM payload `iv:authTag:ciphertext` (crypto.util.ts:37-41) is returned to any workspace member via `POST /workspaces/:id/datasources` and `PATCH /datasources/:id`. The same service deliberately masks the field in `findOne` (line 77) and `findAllByWorkspace` (line 68), so the exposure contradicts the module's own intent. Not decryptable without `DATASOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, but it gives an offline target to anyone who later obtains the key and leaks the credential length via ciphertext size.

verdict.reason: RAW_TEXT_OIDS at datasource.service.ts:21-25 contains only the scalar OIDs DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ (1082/1114/1184); datasourceTypeParser (line 34-37) delegates every other OID to the pg-types default parser, and it is the only parser override on the connection (line 204). A repo-wide grep for setTypeParser/getTypeParser/pg-types/builtins finds no second OID list and no global parser registration, so array OIDs 1182/1115/1185 still hit pg-types' parseDateArray. pg ^8.18.0 (packages/backend/package.json:55) resolves to pg-types@2.2.0 (pnpm-lock.yaml:6987,12185), which registers parseDateArray for those OIDs. Nothing downstream repairs it: executeQuery returns result.rows verbatim (lines 156-165) and toCell (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:32-36) JSON.stringify's the array, serializing each Date via UTC toJSON after it was built in the Node local zone. SET TimeZone='UTC' at line 144 is a server-side session setting only, and there is no process.env.TZ pinning anywhere in the repo (grep: no matches), so the timestamp-without-zone array elements are genuinely reinterpreted in the Node timezone. The reviewer's range-type claim is inaccurate (pg-types 2.2.0 does not parse tsrange/tstzrange/daterange, they stay strings), but the array case alone makes the finding real: SELECT ARRAY['2025-06-15 14:30:00'::timestamp] yields offset-shifted ISO strings in cells. Real wrong-data behavior on a reachable path, within the correctness lane.

verdict.reason: The cited code is present and on the live path: datasource.service.ts:145 unconditionally issues `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` on the connection immediately before executing the user's wrapped SELECT (lines 148-150). In PostgreSQL the second DateStyle field controls ambiguous date *input* parsing, so on a datasource server configured DMY an existing query like `WHERE d = '06/07/2025'` is reinterpreted (June 7 vs July 6), returning silently wrong rows; only the output field was needed, and PostgreSQL allows `SET DateStyle = 'ISO'` to change output alone. The spec at datasource.service.spec.ts:131 pins the exact statement, so it is intentional emitted behavior. samples.summary: Datasource TLS connections disable certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), so a network attacker can MITM and capture the decrypted datasource credentials
samples.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:202 — `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. This is the same `createClient` object literal the diff modifies (it adds `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` at line 204). Vector: a user enables `sslEnabled` believing the connection is authenticated; an attacker on the path between backend and remote Postgres (or who can poison DNS for the user-supplied `host`) presents a self-signed cert. Node accepts it, and the backend then sends `user` plus `decrypt(ds.password)` (line 201) over the attacker-terminated TLS session, handing over plaintext DB credentials and all query results. No CA/hostname option exists in the DTO (datasource.dto.ts has only `sslEnabled`), so verified TLS is unreachable for any caller.

samples.summary: SSRF: fully user-controlled `host`/`port` are dialed by the server and connection errors are reflected verbatim, allowing internal port/service probing and unix-socket access to the app's own database

Any authenticated workspace member POSTs `/workspaces/:id/datasources` then `/datasources/:id/test`; `testConnection` (datasource.service.ts:109-125) returns `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }` straight to the caller, so ECONNREFUSED vs. timeout vs. 'invalid response to SSL negotiation' distinguishes open/closed/non-Postgres internal ports — an internal port scanner with an error oracle. Pointing `host` at the loopback/unix socket plus trust auth or guessed creds reaches the application's own Postgres (all users/tokens). `executeQuery` (line 168) likewise reflects raw pg errors. Pre-existing, but it is the connection path this diff edits and the new e2e tests drive end to end.

If Postgres re-evaluates the GUC rather than keeping the timer armed from statement start, each request pins a backend connection and a remote session indefinitely; repeated requests exhaust connections on both sides. I could not confirm PostgreSQL's mid-statement timer behaviour from the repo, hence low confidence — but nothing in the code prevents the attempt.

samples.summary: `create` and `update` return the datasource row including the encrypted password blob, unlike `findOne`/`findAllByWorkspace` which mask it
samples.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:44-56 (`create`) and 95-98 (`update`) return the Prisma record as-is, so the AES-256-GCM payload `iv:authTag:ciphertext` (crypto.util.ts:37-41) is returned to any workspace member via `POST /workspaces/:id/datasources` and `PATCH /datasources/:id`. The same service deliberately masks the field in `findOne` (line 77) and `findAllByWorkspace` (line 68), so the exposure contradicts the module's own intent. Not decryptable without `DATASOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, but it gives an offline target to anyone who later obtains the key and leaks the credential length via ciphertext size.

finding.summary: Datasource TLS connections disable certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), so a network attacker can MITM and capture the decrypted datasource credentials
finding.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:202 — `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. This is the same `createClient` object literal the diff modifies (it adds `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` at line 204). Vector: a user enables `sslEnabled` believing the connection is authenticated; an attacker on the path between backend and remote Postgres (or who can poison DNS for the user-supplied `host`) presents a self-signed cert. Node accepts it, and the backend then sends `user` plus `decrypt(ds.password)` (line 201) over the attacker-terminated TLS session, handing over plaintext DB credentials and all query results. No CA/hostname option exists in the DTO (datasource.dto.ts has only `sslEnabled`), so verified TLS is unreachable for any caller.

verdict.reason: Verified in the working tree: `createClient` in packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:196-205 builds a pg `Client` with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (line 202) while passing `user: ds.username` and `password: decrypt(ds.password)` (lines 200-201). Certificate verification is therefore disabled on every TLS datasource connection, and there is no CA/servername/hostname-verification option anywhere: the DTOs (packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.dto.ts:39-41, 81-83) expose only a boolean `sslEnabled`, so no caller can request verified TLS. `rejectUnauthorized` appears nowhere else in the repo, so no other code path overrides it. An attacker on the network path (or able to poison DNS for the user-supplied `host`, which is free-form up to 253 chars) can terminate the TLS session with a self-signed certificate; Node accepts it and the backend hands over the decrypted datasource credentials plus all query results. This falls squarely in the crypto/auth lane (weakened certificate verification / credential exposure) and is a clear security weakness, so it is blocking at major severity.

finding.summary: SSRF: fully user-controlled `host`/`port` are dialed by the server and connection errors are reflected verbatim, allowing internal port/service probing and unix-socket access to the app's own database
finding.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.dto.ts:17-25 validates `host` only as a 1-253 char string and `port` only as 1-65535 — no allow-list and no rejection of `localhost`, RFC1918, `169.254.169.254`, or `/var/run/postgresql` (pg treats a host starting with `/` as a unix socket path). Any authenticated workspace member POSTs `/workspaces/:id/datasources` then `/datasources/:id/test`; `testConnection` (datasource.service.ts:109-125) returns `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }` straight to the caller, so ECONNREFUSED vs. timeout vs. 'invalid response to SSL negotiation' distinguishes open/closed/non-Postgres internal ports — an internal port scanner with an error oracle. Pointing `host` at the loopback/unix socket plus trust auth or guessed creds reaches the application's own Postgres (all users/tokens). `executeQuery` (line 168) likewise reflects raw pg errors. Pre-existing, but it is the connection path this diff edits and the new e2e tests drive end to end.

verdict.reason: Verified independently. CreateDataSourceDto/UpdateDataSourceDto (datasource.dto.ts:17-25, 55-64) constrain `host` only by string length (1-253) and `port` only by range 1-65535; there is no allow-list, no loopback/RFC1918/169.254.169.254 rejection, and no rejection of a leading `/` (pg treats such a host as a unix-socket directory, e.g. /var/run/postgresql). createClient (datasource.service.ts:188-206) passes those values straight into `new Client({host, port, ...})`, so the server dials an attacker-chosen internal endpoint. testConnection (datasource.service.ts:109-125) returns `{ success: false, error: (error as Error).message }` verbatim, and executeQuery (datasource.service.ts:166-170) rethrows the raw pg message — giving a distinguishing error oracle (ECONNREFUSED vs connection timeout vs SSL-negotiation errors) that turns this into an internal port/service scanner. The only protection on the path is JwtAuthGuard plus workspaceService.assertMember (datasource.controller.ts:33-44, 120-131, 133-145), which any authenticated user trivially satisfies in a workspace they own, so it does not constrain egress. A repo-wide grep for host allow/deny logic under packages/backend/src found no SSRF guard anywhere (only unrelated config/test fixtures). This is SSRF plus sensitive error-detail exposure — squarely in the Security lane, with major/critical impact potential (reaching the app's own Postgres via loopback/unix socket).

finding.summary: Read-only enforcement is a SQL keyword blocklist only; the newly added session `SET` block omits `default_transaction_read_only`, so side-effecting functions inside a SELECT can still write to the connected database
finding.evidence: packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.service.ts:143-145 now issues three session settings (`statement_timeout`, `TimeZone`, `DateStyle`) but not `SET default_transaction_read_only = on` / `SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, the only enforcement Postgres itself honours. Enforcement therefore rests entirely on packages/backend/src/datasource/sql-validator.ts:1-13, a substring blocklist of DML keywords. A workspace member — not necessarily the credential owner, since `/datasources/:id/query` only requires `assertMember` (datasource.controller.ts:133-145) — can submit `SELECT * FROM (SELECT my_volatile_writer()) x`, `SELECT nextval('some_seq')`, `SELECT lo_import('/etc/passwd')`, `SELECT pg_read_file(...)` or `SELECT dblink(...)`: none contain a forbidden keyword, all pass validation and are executed at line 150 inside the `SELECT * FROM (...)` wrapper, producing writes, local file reads (superuser) or outbound connections on the remote database.
searchedFor: read datasource.service.ts and datasource.controller.ts in full for other enforcement layers
glob packages/backend/src/datasource/** to enumerate the module

verdict.reason: Verified independently: read-only intent is enforced only by the keyword blocklist in sql-validator.ts (FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS at :1-13, applied at :46-57) plus a first-token SELECT/WITH check. The session setup in datasource.service.ts:142-145 issues only statement_timeout, TimeZone and DateStyle — no `SET default_transaction_read_only = on`, no `SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, no `BEGIN ... READ ONLY`; and createClient (:196-206) passes no `options: '-c default_transaction_read_only=on'`. Repo-wide greps for default_transaction_read_only / transaction_read_only / 'BEGIN READ ONLY' / 'SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS' / "options: '-c" and an enumeration of every client.query / new Client( call site across all packages produced no enforcement layer anywhere; the unit spec (datasource.service.spec.ts:129-132) asserts exactly those three SETs and then the wrapped query, confirming no fourth setting. Consequently a query such as `SELECT nextval('s')`, `SELECT pg_read_file(...)`, `SELECT dblink(...)` or `SELECT volatile_writer()` contains no blocklisted token, passes validateSelectQuery, and is executed at datasource.service.ts:150 inside `SELECT * FROM (...) AS _q LIMIT` — side effects commit in the implicit transaction. The stated reachability also holds: /datasources/:id/query is gated by assertMember only (datasource.controller.ts:133-145) and ExecuteQueryDto accepts arbitrary SQL up to 100k chars (datasource.dto.ts:86-90), so any workspace member (not just the credential owner) can drive it. In-lane for Security as unsafe input handling / bypassable SQL gate; no counterexample found.
